extracted.intended_audience: amateur shell-collectors and naturalists (beginners and students)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for locating, identifying, collecting, killing, cleaning, storing, and labelling marine, freshwater, and land mollusc shells for an amateur collection. Emphasis on field methods, distinguishing morphological features, and simple preservation techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marine shells: search and retrieval methods
rubrics_metrics.description: MARINE SHELLS may be obtained, 1st, by searching on and under rocks at low water, or on coral reefs, among seaweed attached to them, or floating on the sea, or on a sandy beach. Bivalves may be found by digging in the sand, or mud, on a beach, or at the mouth of a river: their presence is generally indicated by a circular breathing hole in the sand. 2nd. By dredging, by which means only deep-sea shells can be obtained; but after a storm these may often be found upon the shore, before they have lost their lustre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detach limpets etc. with a thin blade passed quickly under the shell, taking care not to break the edges. Small shells on and in seaweed, and limpets, etc., adhering to stones will drop off and sink to the bottom in a vessel of cold fresh water. Note: 'hot water often destroys their lustre' — avoid hot-water cleaning for marine shells.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freshwater shells: capture techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: FRESH-WATER SHELLS may be obtained in any river, lake, pond, marsh or reservoir. Univalves, chiefly on the banks, on reeds and plants growing near the hedges, and on the under surface, leaves, and stems of aquatic plants. Bivalves generally at the bottom, among stones, or buried in the sand, or among the roots of aquatic plants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best captured by means of a perforated scoop whether they are on the waterweeds or hidden in the sand or mud of the bottom. Note the advice that freshwater shells include univalves and bivalves and are often greenish-brown as protective colouring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Land shells: habitats and timing for collecting
rubrics_metrics.description: LAND SHELLS mostly abound in a chalk or limestone district, and in moist and wooded situations. Some species inhabit low and damp spots, roots of trees, hollows and crevices of rocks and walls; some lie under stones or pieces of wood, or in the earth; others climb shrubs. Their haunts vary according to the weather and the season. They come out early in the morning, and after rain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for them under stones, wood or in moss; search on damp nights for subterranean species (e.g. Testacella). Collect the smallest shells, especially young imperfect shells. Note local preferences (chalk, lime, coal measures, etc.) when choosing search areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer live shells; criteria for choosing dead shells
rubrics_metrics.description: In all cases "live shells," i.e. shells in which the animal is alive, are to be chosen; but, when these cannot be procured, "dead shells," which have not lost their lustre, or their colour, especially those of rare species, should be preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise live specimens for collections. If keeping dead specimens, select those that retain lustre and colour (important for rare species).

rubrics_metrics.name: Killing and removing animals from shells
rubrics_metrics.description: The animals of Land and Freshwater shells may be killed by immersing them for a few minutes in boiling water, after which the bodies may be easily extracted whole with any suitable instrument, e.g., a fork or a pin, according to size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use boiling water for land and freshwater molluscs to allow whole-body extraction. Do not use hot water for marine shells because it often destroys their lustre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cleaning shells: minimal intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: No attempt should be made to clean them, or to remove the furry skin, more or less thick, with which they are often covered, beyond removing with a soft brush any mud or sand adhering to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit cleaning to gentle removal of mud/sand with a soft brush; avoid stripping natural coverings or using harsh treatments that could damage colour or surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storage methods: tubes, matchboxes, and trays
rubrics_metrics.description: As to the arrangement of shells in a collection before a regular cabinet is obtained, the tinier shells may be kept in small glass tubes with corks (such as used for homoeopathic medicines), and the medium sized ones in the trays of common matchboxes, these being arranged in large shallow glass-covered trays which can be obtained from any cardboard boxmaker at a small cost, and several of these, stored one above the other, form an excellent substitute for a more costly cabinet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use glass tubes for tiniest shells, matchbox trays for medium shells, and stack trays in glass-covered shallow trays as an inexpensive cabinet alternative. Include actual-size indication where possible for reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Label specimens with name and locality
rubrics_metrics.description: In all cases the name, and the place where the shells were found, should be written on a small slip of card placed in the tube or tray.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always record taxonomy and exact find-location on a slip placed with the specimen; this is essential for scientific value and exchange/records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mounting fastenings: avoid gluing; use gum tragacanth if needed
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not well in most cases to fasten the shells on card, but if this is done gum tragacanth is best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer loose storage over mounting on card. If mounting is necessary, use gum tragacanth rather than harsher adhesives to avoid damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation environment: protect from damp and dust
rubrics_metrics.description: The collection should be kept free from damp and from dust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Store trays/cabinets in dry, clean conditions to prevent mold, deterioration, or soiling of shells.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine minute shells with magnifier
rubrics_metrics.description: All the Pupæ should be examined with a magnifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a magnifying glass to see characteristic denticles in the mouth and presence/absence of striations for minute species; enlargements help distinguish very small species.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification by morphological and habit characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use shell features (shape, whorls, umbilicus, aperture/peristome shape and rim, denticles, operculum, surface texture, presence of hairs, glossiness, banding and colour variation), and habits/habitats (e.g., subterranean, amphibious, gregariousness, food preferences, seasonal activity) to distinguish species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text provides many species-specific diagnostic notes (e.g., hidden umbilicus in Cryptomphalus aspersa, 89 possible band variations in Cepæa nemoralis, clausilium in Clausilia family, operculum presence in Pomatias and Acicula). Use a combination of external morphology and known habitat/distribution for reliable identification; consult illustrations and measure whorl counts where indicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting tiny and young imperfect shells
rubrics_metrics.description: The smallest shells, especially of land species, and young imperfect shells should be collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ignore minute or juvenile specimens; they are important for completeness of a collection and may require magnification for study.
